 The Social Security trust funds, OASI and DI, pay different benefits from separate accounts — here is who each covers, how they are funded and what the 2025 Trustees Report projects
 1 / 12 List slides OASI vs. DI: what separates Social Security's 2 trust funds List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 12, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The date most often attached to Social Security's financial future describes an account that does not legally exist. When the 2025 Trustees Report projected that reserves would last until 2034, that date applied to a hypothetical combined fund. The program actually runs on two Social Security trust funds, each legally separate and held in the U.S. Treasury. Their outlooks are far apart.
 The first is the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund, known as OASI. It pays retirement benefits to workers and their eligible family members. It also pays benefits to the families of workers who have died. The second is the Disability Insurance trust fund, or DI. It pays workers whose medical conditions keep them from substantial work, along with their eligible dependents. The two are often analyzed together under the label OASDI. Each fund still keeps its own accounts and can pay only what it holds.
 That separation shapes how the program's finances look. Under the 2025 Trustees Report, the OASI fund is projected to pay full benefits until 2033, a year earlier than the combined figure. The DI fund is not projected to be depleted at all within the report's 75-year window. A single combined date blends those two different paths into one number.
 The distinction matters to anyone planning around the program. A retiree, a surviving spouse and a disabled worker draw on different pools of money. Both pools receive revenue from the same payroll tax, and Congress decides how that tax is divided between them. Lawmakers have redirected payroll tax revenue from one fund to the other before. Any borrowing between the funds today would require Congress to act.
 The trust funds are also often confused with programs they do not pay for. Supplemental Security Income, a means-tested program funded by general Treasury revenue, is not paid from either trust fund. Medicare's Hospital Insurance program has a trust fund of its own.
 The 10 slides below explain what each fund is, who it pays, where its money comes from and how it is invested. They also cover when each fund was created and the 2015 law that delayed a projected DI shortfall. Later slides look at borrowing between the two funds, the latest projections from the Board of Trustees and the programs neither fund pays for.
 What OASI and DI mean in Social Security's trust funds 
 Illustration: Quartz
 OASI stands for Old-Age and Survivors Insurance, and DI stands for Disability Insurance. They are two legally separate trust funds in the U.S. Treasury. Together they finance the monthly cash benefits most people simply call Social Security.
 Each name describes the risk its fund covers. "Old-age" refers to benefits paid in retirement. "Survivors" refers to the family members left behind when a worker dies. "Disability" refers to workers whose medical conditions keep them from substantial work before they reach full retirement age.
 Put the two together and the result is OASDI, short for Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance. That is the formal name of the program. It is also the label used when government actuaries, analysts and lawmakers look at both funds as a single unit.
 The word "separate" has a specific meaning here. Each fund keeps its own books, with its own income and its own outgoing payments. A retiree's or a surviving spouse's monthly check is charged to OASI. Payments to a disabled worker and that worker's eligible dependents are charged to DI.
 That separation has a legal edge. Federal law does not allow either fund to pay benefits beyond what it holds. A large balance in one fund does not raise the amount the other can pay.
 The separation also explains why projections are reported two ways. Social Security's trustees publish an outlook for each fund on its own. Their report comes out once a year. They also publish figures for a combined OASDI fund. That combined fund is hypothetical. It does not exist as an account, and no benefit is paid from it.
 The labels carry weight because the two funds' outlooks can differ. A report on Social Security's finances may describe OASI, DI or the hypothetical combination of both. Each of those carries its own projections. The fund name tells a reader which set of numbers applies.
 Who receives benefits from the OASI trust fund 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund pays monthly benefits to retired workers, their eligible spouses and children, and the surviving families of workers who have died.
 The fund's name describes its two jobs. "Old-age" refers to retirement benefits that workers claim based on their own covered earnings. "Survivors" refers to the family members a worker leaves behind. They can collect benefits based on that worker's record.
 Retirement claims follow an age schedule set in law. The earliest age to claim a Social Security retirement benefit is 62. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Those two ages frame a retiree's decision about when to start drawing from OASI.
 Full retirement age is tied to the year of birth, so the schedule is not identical for every worker. A person born in 1960 or later faces a five-year span between the earliest claiming age and full retirement age. Where a claim falls inside that span is a choice each retiree makes.
 Family benefits for a living retiree rest on that retiree's work history. An eligible spouse or child does not need a separate account in his or her own name to receive a payment. The money is tied to the retired worker's earnings record and paid from the same fund.
 Survivor benefits apply the same principle after a death. When a covered worker dies, eligible members of the surviving family can receive monthly payments from OASI. The fund therefore supports households that lose a worker, not only people who reach retirement age. A surviving child can draw on the fund long before reaching retirement age.
 That range of beneficiaries sets OASI apart from the Disability Insurance trust fund. A retiree, the retiree's spouse, a dependent child and the widow or widower of a deceased worker can all receive payments traced to the same Old-Age and Survivors Insurance account.
 The fund's financial outlook therefore reaches well beyond retirees. Retirees and survivors draw on one pool. Any projection about OASI reserves applies to survivor benefits as much as to retirement benefits.
 Who qualifies for payments from the Disability Insurance trust fund 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Disability Insurance trust fund pays monthly benefits to disabled workers and to their eligible dependents. A worker qualifies by meeting the Social Security Administration's definition of disability. That means a medical condition that prevents substantial gainful activity and is expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death.
 The definition has two parts, and a claimant must meet both. The first concerns work. It asks whether the condition keeps a person from engaging in substantial gainful activity, the Social Security Administration's term for significant paid work. A medical diagnosis alone does not settle the question.
 The second part concerns time. The condition must be expected to last at least a year or to end in death. An illness or injury expected to clear up within a few months falls outside that standard, even if it keeps someone off the job while it lasts. A condition expected to result in death meets the time test without any minimum duration.
 Benefits do not begin as soon as a qualifying disability starts. A five-month waiting period applies first. The fund pays nothing for those first five months of disability.
 Coverage extends beyond the worker. Eligible dependents of a disabled worker can also receive monthly payments. Those family benefits come from the Disability Insurance trust fund, not from the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund.
 Disability Insurance has an end point built in. When a disabled worker reaches full retirement age, the disability benefit converts to a retirement benefit. From that point on, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund pays it. The beneficiary still receives a monthly payment, but the account it comes from changes.
 That handoff divides the cost of a disabled worker's benefits between the two funds over time. Disability Insurance carries the payments in the years before full retirement age. Old-Age and Survivors Insurance carries them from full retirement age onward.
 How the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax feeds OASI and DI 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Most of the money flowing into Social Security's two trust funds comes from a 12.4% payroll tax on covered earnings. That single rate is divided between the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund and the Disability Insurance fund in proportions set by Congress.
 For a typical employee, the tax is shared. The worker pays 6.2% of covered wages, and the employer pays a matching 6.2%. The worker's half is withheld from each paycheck. The employer's half is paid on top of wages and does not show up as a deduction on the employee's pay stub.
 A worker with $50,000 in covered wages for the year pays $3,100 toward Social Security. The employer adds another $3,100. Together, $6,200 from that one job goes toward the two funds.
 Self-employed people work under a different arrangement. They pay the full 12.4% themselves. A self-employed person carries both the worker share and the employer share instead of splitting the rate with an employer.
 The tax does not apply to every dollar a person earns. It stops at an annual ceiling called the taxable maximum, which is $176,100 for 2025. Earnings above that line are not subject to the Social Security payroll tax. An employee with covered wages at or above $176,100 pays $10,918.20 for 2025, and the employer pays the same amount.
 The ceiling is not fixed. It is adjusted each year in line with growth in average wages. As pay across the economy rises, the cap rises with it.
 The split between the two funds is written into law. It is not a decision the Social Security Administration makes on its own. Congress has changed the division over time. Those changes have steered a larger or smaller slice of the rate toward disability benefits or toward retirement and survivor benefits. A shift in the split moves money between the funds without changing the combined 12.4% rate a worker pays.
 Payroll tax is not the only revenue stream. Some beneficiaries owe federal income tax on part of their Social Security benefits. That income tax revenue also flows into the trust funds.
 How the trust funds hold money in special-issue Treasury securities 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security's trust funds hold their reserves in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, and those holdings earn interest. Benefits and administrative costs are paid out of the funds. Federal law does not allow either fund to pay benefits beyond what it holds.
 The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) trust fund and the Disability Insurance (DI) trust fund each keep their own holdings. The two are legally separate accounts inside the U.S. Treasury. A security credited to one fund belongs to that fund alone. The interest it pays goes to that fund alone as well.
 The term trust fund can suggest a vault of cash or a diversified portfolio of stocks and corporate bonds. Neither picture fits. OASI and DI reserves sit in Treasury securities issued specifically to the trust funds. That is what the special-issue label refers to.
 Money moves through each fund in two directions. On the income side, the funds receive payroll tax revenue, income taxes paid on part of some beneficiaries' benefits and interest on the securities they already hold. On the spending side, the funds pay monthly benefits and cover the cost of administering the program.
 Interest differs from the other two income sources because it depends on the reserve itself. When a fund holds securities, the interest those securities earn is credited back to that fund. All else equal, a larger reserve produces more interest income, and a shrinking reserve produces less.
 The spending limit gives the reserve its practical weight. A fund's balance of Treasury securities, together with the income still arriving, sets the ceiling on what that fund can pay at any point.
 The same rule explains why the two funds are tracked separately rather than as one pool. Each fund's ability to pay depends on its own holdings and its own income. A surplus in one fund does not automatically cover a gap in the other. For that reason, the condition of OASI and the condition of DI are reported as distinct figures.
 When Congress created the OASI and DI trust funds 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund dates to 1939, when amendments to the Social Security Act added survivor benefits. The Disability Insurance trust fund followed 17 years later, in 1956.
 The program itself is older than either fund. The Social Security Act was signed in 1935, four years before the OASI trust fund began. The 1939 amendments widened the program's reach beyond the individual worker. Benefits could now go to the family a deceased worker left behind.
 The fund created by that change carries both groups in its name. "Old age" points to retired workers. "Survivors" points to the family members the 1939 amendments brought into the program.
 From 1939 until 1956, OASI was Social Security's only trust fund. Retirement and survivor benefits drew on a single account during those 17 years.
 That changed in 1956, when Congress created the Disability Insurance trust fund. Money for disability benefits was placed in an account of its own in the U.S. Treasury, separate from retirement and survivor money. From that point, Social Security operated with two legally separate trust funds. The same two-fund structure remains in place today.
 The order of these steps traces how the program's idea of risk widened. The 1935 law began with the worker's own old age. The 1939 changes reached the worker's family after a death. The 1956 fund addressed a loss of earnings that can arrive during a working life rather than at its end.
 The combined label OASDI records that history. Its letters follow the order in which the benefits were added, with disability last. Reading the acronym left to right gives a short timeline of how the program grew from 1935 to 1956.
 The 1956 split also drew a legal line between the two pools of money. Moving resources across that line has required action by Congress. A shortfall in one fund cannot simply be covered from the other without new legislation.
 How the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 delayed DI fund depletion 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 kept the Disability Insurance trust fund from running short in late 2016. It temporarily sent a larger share of the Social Security payroll tax to DI and a smaller share to the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund for 2016 through 2018.
 The deadline came from the 2015 Trustees Report. That annual report projected DI reserves would run short in late 2016. Congress acted the same year the projection appeared.
 A shortfall would have had direct consequences for beneficiaries. Federal law does not allow the trust funds to pay benefits beyond what they hold. Had DI reserves run out, the fund could have paid only what its incoming revenue covered. Disabled workers and their dependents would have received reduced payments instead of full scheduled benefits.
 The fix was not a tax increase. The combined payroll tax stayed at 12.4% of covered earnings, with employees and employers each paying 6.2%. What changed was how that rate was divided between the two funds. Congress sets that division by law, and the split has shifted at other points in the program's history. The 2015 act used that authority to steer revenue toward the fund facing the nearer shortfall.
 OASI absorbed the other side of the shift. During 2016, 2017 and 2018, OASI collected less payroll tax income than it would have under the prior split, and DI collected more. The total amount workers and employers paid did not change.
 A reallocation is also distinct from interfund borrowing. It changes where new tax revenue goes. It creates no loan between the funds and leaves nothing to repay.
 The arrangement carried an end date written into the law. It covered three years and pushed back the date DI was projected to run short. The Trustees revisit that projection in each new Trustees Report, which is how the effect of the 2015 change shows up in later forecasts.
 Interfund borrowing between OASI and DI explained 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Interfund borrowing lets one Social Security trust fund draw on another fund's reserves when its own run low, with the loan repaid later. The law has permitted such borrowing in the past, but any loan between OASI and DI today would require Congress to act.
 The two funds need this mechanism because they are legally separate. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund and the Disability Insurance trust fund each keep their own accounts in the U.S. Treasury. Money credited to one does not automatically cover a gap in the other. A fund with larger reserves cannot shore up the other unless lawmakers authorize a transfer.
 One precedent dates to the early 1980s. During that period, the OASI trust fund borrowed from other trust funds. Those loans were repaid by 1986. The arrangement was temporary, and the retirement fund returned what it had drawn within a few years.
 The 1980s episode also shows which side of the program has needed help before. The borrower then was the retirement and survivors fund. Under the 2025 Trustees Report, OASI is again the fund projected to run short first.
 Borrowing does not create new money for Social Security. A loan shifts reserves from one account to another, so the program's total reserves stay the same. It can postpone the date a single fund runs short. It cannot add to what the two funds hold together.
 A loan works differently from a reallocation. A reallocation, such as the one in the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, changes how incoming payroll tax revenue is divided between the funds. Borrowing instead moves reserves a fund already holds, and the money is expected to come back.
 The 2025 Trustees Report also presents a hypothetical combined OASDI fund. That measure treats the two funds' reserves as a single pool for analysis. It does not describe money that can move between them under current law. Pooling the reserves in practice would take legislation, whether new borrowing authority, a reallocation or another change to the program.
 What the 2025 Trustees Report projects for OASI and DI 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 2025 Trustees Report projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund can pay full scheduled benefits until 2033. The Disability Insurance trust fund is in a different position. The report does not project it to be depleted at any point in its 75-year projection window.
 Once the OASI reserves run out, the 2025 report projects that incoming revenue would cover about 77% of scheduled OASI benefits. Payments to retired workers, their eligible family members and survivors would then face a reduction of about 23% if Congress does not act before 2033.
 Depletion of a trust fund does not mean benefits stop. Workers and employers keep paying payroll taxes after the reserves are gone. That ongoing revenue would still fund most scheduled OASI benefits. The gap applies to the portion that the reserves had been covering.
 Many summaries of Social Security's finances cite a single combined OASDI estimate. That figure pools OASI and DI reserves on paper, as if they sat in one account. Under the 2025 report, such a hypothetical combined fund could pay about 81% of scheduled benefits once its reserves ran out.
 The combined estimate is an analytical tool, not a real account. OASI and DI are legally separate funds. For retirement and survivor benefits, the relevant figure is the OASI projection of about 77%, not the combined 81%.
 The DI projection in the 2025 report covers only benefits paid from the disability fund. It is calculated from that fund's own income and costs, apart from the OASI timeline.
 The projections come from the Social Security Board of Trustees, which issues a new report every year. The board has six members. They are the Treasury secretary, who serves as managing trustee, the Labor secretary, the secretary of Health and Human Services, the Social Security commissioner and two public trustees. Each projection carries its report year, and a later edition can revise these dates.
 What OASI and DI do not pay for: SSI and Medicare 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, is not paid from either Social Security trust fund. It is funded by general revenue from the U.S. Treasury and is means-tested. Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund is also a separate account from both OASI and DI.
 Funding is the first dividing line between SSI and the two trust funds. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds collect dedicated income. That money comes from the Social Security payroll tax on covered earnings, from income taxes on part of some beneficiaries' benefits and from interest on the funds' holdings. SSI receives none of it. Its payments come from the government's general Treasury revenue rather than from a tax set aside for the program.
 Means-testing is the second dividing line. SSI eligibility depends on a person's income and resources. OASI and DI apply no means test. Their benefits go to workers and eligible family members, and the money behind them comes from payroll taxes on covered earnings.
 SSI and DI can both pay people with disabilities, but they are separate programs with separate money. The Social Security Administration runs all three programs, so they share an agency but not a funding source. A person receiving SSI is not drawing on the DI trust fund. Projections about DI's reserves therefore have no direct bearing on SSI payments.
 Medicare sits outside both Social Security funds as well. Its Hospital Insurance trust fund is accounted for separately from OASI and DI. Depletion dates published for Social Security's trust funds describe only OASI, DI and their combined OASDI total. They do not describe the reserves behind Medicare's hospital coverage.
 Any trust fund projection applies only to the account it covers. A figure for OASI does not transfer to DI. Neither applies to SSI, which has no trust fund of its own, or to Medicare's hospital fund.
